html:
The walled imperial palace at the heart of Beijing, built from 1406 to 1420 by the Yongle Emperor of the Ming dynasty. It was the home and seat of government of Chinese emperors for almost five hundred years.

Yongle had seized the throne from his nephew and decided to move the capital from Nanjing to Beijing, his old power base near the northern frontier. The palace was the centrepiece. Behind a moat and high red walls lie close to a thousand buildings, laid out on a strict north to south axis. The great halls of the outer court served for ceremonies; the inner court was the private world of the emperor, his women and eunuchs. Ordinary people could not enter, hence the name.

Twenty-four emperors of the Ming and Qing lived here. After the Xinhai Revolution the last emperor, Puyi, was allowed to stay until 1924. The next year it opened as the Palace Museum. It is the largest surviving palace complex in the world.
